title: Can Small Vision-Language Models Explain Career Maps? Reading the Picture or the Data behind a Sankey Diagram
content: Career guidance platforms such as XR-CareerAssist show possible careers as Sankey diagrams, in which bands of varying width show how many people moved between roles or industries over 2, 5 and 10 years. A virtual assistant that explains such a map can read the picture with a vision-language model or read the table of numbers behind it. This paper compares the two on SankeyQA, a new open benchmark of 600 simulated career maps with 6,560 questions whose answers are computed exactly from the underlying tables, so that no personal data are needed. Five small open models that run on a laptop processor answered 875 questions about 80 unseen maps. A direct look-up in the table was always right. The best picture reader, SmolVLM-500M, answered 30.1% of the questions correctly and a small language model reading the table 38.9%, while a guess that never looks at the map reached 40.5%. The picture readers could not read the numbers printed in the maps and rarely followed flows correctly. Fine-tuning BLIP on 400 maps raised its accuracy from 12.7% to 55.5%, and 20 maps chosen for diversity by k-means were no better than 20 random maps. An assistant that explains career maps should therefore answer from the data and use the picture to show the answer. The benchmark, the code and all model replies are openly available.
